lessons.title: Water Quality for Seedlings
lessons.body: Water quality is critical for healthy seedlings. The best water is clean, free from salt, and at a comfortable temperature. Rainwater is ideal because it is soft and free of chemicals. If you use tap water, let it sit in an open container for 24 hours to allow chlorine to evaporate. Well water or borehole water may be high in salts or minerals; test it by checking for white crust on pots or leaf tips. If you see crust, switch to rainwater or mix with rainwater. Avoid using water from rivers or dams that may contain disease organisms or pollution. If you must, filter it through a cloth and let it settle, then use only the clear top portion. Water temperature matters: cold water can shock seedlings, especially in the morning. Let water warm to air temperature before use. In hot climates, water early morning or late evening to reduce evaporation and heat stress. For small nurseries, a simple test: fill a clear bottle with water, let it stand, and check for sediment or odour. If it smells bad or looks cloudy, do not use it. You can also use a cheap TDS meter (total dissolved solids) to check salt levels; aim for less than 500 ppm. If water is too salty, seedlings will wilt even when soil is wet. Always store water in clean containers, covered to prevent mosquito breeding and algae growth. For African farms, harvesting rainwater from roofs into tanks or drums is a low-cost solution. A 200-litre drum can water many seedlings. Remember, clean water prevents diseases like damping-off and root rot. If you notice white mould on soil surface, it may be from dirty water or overwatering. Change water source and improve drainage.

lessons.title: Manual Watering Techniques
lessons.body: Manual watering is the most common method for small nurseries. The goal is to water gently and evenly without disturbing seeds or seedlings. Use a watering can with a fine rose (the sprinkler head) to break the water flow. A 5-litre can is easy to handle. For very small seedlings, a spray bottle works well. Water in the morning if possible, so leaves dry before evening and diseases are less likely. If you water in the evening, avoid wetting the leaves. Check soil moisture by sticking your finger 2 cm into the soil. If it feels dry, water. If it feels moist, wait. For seed trays, water until water runs out the bottom, then stop. This ensures the entire root zone is moist. Do not blast water; it can wash seeds away or knock over seedlings. For larger pots, water around the base of the plant, not on the leaves. A simple test: lift the pot. A dry pot is light; a wet pot is heavy. This helps you know when to water. In hot, dry areas, you may need to water twice a day: early morning and late afternoon. In cooler or rainy weather, water less. Always use clean water at room temperature. If you have many seedlings, set up a routine: water one section at a time, and check each tray. Avoid walking on wet soil as it compacts it. For hanging baskets or vertical gardens, use a small cup to pour water slowly. If you see water pooling on the surface, stop and let it soak in, then continue. This prevents runoff. After watering, empty saucers under pots to avoid root rot. If you use a hose, attach a spray nozzle and keep pressure low. Never use a strong jet. For African farmers, a simple DIY watering can from a plastic bottle with holes in the cap works for small numbers. Remember, consistent moisture is key. Do not let seedlings dry out completely, but do not keep them soggy.

lessons.title: Setting Up a Simple Drip Irrigation System
lessons.body: Drip irrigation saves water and labour. You can build a simple system for a small nursery using locally available materials. You need: a water source (tank or drum) elevated at least 1 metre, a main line of 16mm black polyethylene tubing, drip lines (thin tubes with emitters), and connectors. A 200-litre drum placed on a stand 1.5 metres high provides enough pressure for 10-20 metres of drip line. Start by connecting a filter to the tank outlet to prevent clogging. Then run the main line along the nursery beds. Punch holes in the main line where you want drip lines, and insert barbed connectors. Attach drip lines (often 6mm) that run along each row of seedlings. Space emitters according to plant needs: for seedlings in trays, use one emitter per tray or a micro-sprinkler. You can also make DIY emitters by poking small holes in a hose, but these clog easily. Better to buy inexpensive inline drip tape with built-in emitters every 30 cm. For a 10-metre bed, you might need 10 metres of drip tape. Connect the end of each drip line to a flush cap for cleaning. Turn on the water and check that all emitters are working. If some are dry, they may be clogged; clean or replace. Run the system for 10-15 minutes and check soil moisture. You can attach a simple tap timer to automate watering, but manual on/off is fine. In Africa, many farmers use gravity-fed drip kits from local agrovets. Costs: a basic kit for 50 seedlings may cost $20-30. Maintenance: flush lines weekly, clean filter, and check for leaks. Drip irrigation reduces water use by up to 50% compared to manual watering. It also keeps leaves dry, reducing disease. For very small nurseries, you can use a bucket with a small hole and a string wick to each pot, but drip is more reliable. Always use clean water to avoid clogging. If water is dirty, pre-filter through cloth.

lessons.title: Misting and Humidity Control
lessons.body: Seedlings, especially young ones, need high humidity to thrive. Misting mimics dew and prevents leaves from drying out. Use a hand-held spray bottle or a misting nozzle on a hose. Mist lightly in the morning and early afternoon, not in the evening to avoid fungal diseases. For a small nursery, a simple misting system can be made with a 5-litre sprayer. Fill with clean water and pump to pressurize. Spray a fine mist over the seedlings, holding the nozzle 30-40 cm away. You want the leaves to be slightly wet but not dripping. In hot, dry climates, you may need to mist 2-3 times a day. In humid areas, once a day is enough. To increase humidity around seedlings, you can place trays on a bed of wet gravel or use a humidome (a clear plastic cover) over seed trays. But be careful: too much humidity causes mould. Remove covers for a few hours each day to allow air circulation. A simple hygrometer (humidity meter) costs a few dollars and helps you monitor. Aim for 60-80% relative humidity for most seedlings. If humidity is too low, leaves curl and edges turn brown. If too high, you see fuzzy mould or algae. For African conditions, a shade net over the nursery helps retain humidity and reduces evaporation. You can also group pots together to create a microclimate. Misting is not the same as watering; it does not replace watering the soil. Always check soil moisture separately. For seedlings in a greenhouse, you can set up a fogger or misting system with a timer, but that is more advanced. Start with manual misting. A simple trick: hang wet burlap sacks around the nursery to increase humidity as they dry. Replace or rewet them daily. Remember, good air movement is also important to prevent diseases. So balance humidity with ventilation. If you see condensation on leaves in the morning, that is good. If you see water sitting on leaves for hours, reduce misting.

lessons.title: Avoiding Overwatering and Underwatering
lessons.body: Overwatering and underwatering are the most common mistakes in seedling nurseries. Both stress plants and reduce survival. Overwatering symptoms: yellowing leaves, wilting despite wet soil, mould on soil surface, and root rot. The soil feels soggy and may smell bad. Underwatering symptoms: dry, crispy leaves, wilting that does not recover after watering, and slow growth. The soil is dry and pulls away from pot edges. To avoid overwatering, always check soil moisture before watering. Stick your finger 2 cm into the soil. If it is moist, do not water. If it is dry, water. For small trays, you can also lift them: a light tray is dry, a heavy one is wet. Water only until water runs out the bottom, then stop. Never let pots sit in water; empty saucers after 30 minutes. Use well-draining soil mix: add sand or perlite to improve drainage. In rainy seasons, protect seedlings from heavy rain with a cover or move them under shelter. To avoid underwatering, water consistently. In hot weather, check twice a day. Use a schedule but adjust based on weather. For example, water every morning, but if it is very hot and windy, also check in the afternoon. Mulching around pots or beds helps retain moisture. For seedlings in trays, a fine mist may not be enough; you need to water the soil. A simple test: after watering, wait 1 hour and check if the soil is moist at 2 cm depth. If not, water more. If it is soggy, you overwatered. Keep a notebook to track watering and plant response. This helps you learn. In Africa, where temperatures can be extreme, underwatering is more common in dry seasons, but overwatering can happen in wet seasons or with poor drainage. Always use pots with drainage holes. If you see algae on soil, it means too much water. If you see ants or dry soil, it means too little. Adjust immediately. Healthy seedlings have firm stems and green leaves. If they look stressed, check water first.

lessons.title: Watering Schedules for Different Growth Stages
lessons.body: Seedlings have different water needs at each growth stage. Germination: seeds need constant moisture but not soggy. Water lightly twice a day with a fine mist until seeds sprout. Keep the soil surface moist. Once sprouts appear, reduce to once a day. For most vegetables, germination takes 5-10 days. After germination (cotyledon stage): water gently once a day, preferably morning. The soil should be moist but not dripping. Avoid overhead watering that can knock over seedlings; use a watering can with a fine rose or bottom watering. For bottom watering, place trays in a shallow pan of water for 10 minutes, then remove. This encourages deep roots. True leaf stage (2-4 leaves): water once a day, increasing amount as roots grow. Check soil moisture daily. In hot weather, you may need to water twice. At this stage, you can start using a drip system. Transplant stage (4-6 leaves): water deeply before transplanting to reduce shock. After transplanting, water daily for the first week, then every 2-3 days. The goal is to encourage roots to grow deep. For seedlings in trays, water when the top 1 cm of soil is dry. In general, a schedule: Week 1: mist twice daily. Week 2: water once daily. Week 3-4: water once daily, more if hot. Week 5-6: water every 1-2 days. Always adjust based on weather, soil type, and plant type. For example, tomatoes need more water than succulents. In dry season, increase frequency; in rainy season, reduce. A simple rule: water in the morning so leaves dry before night. If you use a timer for drip, set it for 10-15 minutes per day for young seedlings, and 20-30 minutes for older ones. But always check soil moisture. Keep a record of your schedule and note any changes. For African farmers, a good practice is to water before 9 AM and after 4 PM if needed. Never water in the heat of the day. As seedlings grow, their root systems expand, so water less often but more deeply. This encourages strong roots. By the time they are ready for the field, they should be hardened off with less frequent watering.

lessons.title: Practical Reference
lessons.body:
Practical Reference: Watering and Irrigation for Seedling Nurseries

Water is the single most controllable input in a seedling nursery â and the one most often wasted, misapplied, or contaminated. For African agribusinesses producing vegetable, tree, or fodder seedlings for sale, water management directly determines germination rates, seedling uniformity, transplant survival, and ultimately your profit margin per tray. A nursery that loses 30% of seedlings to damping-off or drought stress is not a nursery; it is an expense. This practical reference consolidates the operational knowledge from the six lessons in this module into a single field-ready guide: water quality thresholds, manual and drip application methods, humidity control, stress diagnosis, and stage-specific scheduling.

1. Water Quality: The Invisible Input

Seedlings are more sensitive to water quality than mature plants because their root volume is tiny and their buffer capacity is near zero. Three parameters matter most in African nursery contexts: salinity (measured as electrical conductivity, EC), sodium hazard (sodium adsorption ratio, SAR), and biological contamination. Borehole water in the Sahel, Rift Valley, and parts of Southern Africa frequently exceeds 1.0 dS/m EC, which is tolerable for mature tomatoes but damaging for germinating seedlings. Surface water from rivers, dams, or open tanks is the primary vector for Pythium, Phytophthora, and Fusarium â the pathogens behind damping-off.

Practical rule: if your water source is a borehole with EC above 0.75 dS/m, blend it with rainwater harvested from nursery roofs, or leach trays periodically. If your source is open surface water, treat it â chlorination at 2â5 mg/L free chlorine, or solarization in clear 20-litre bottles for 6 hours of full sun, both work at small scale.

Table 1: Water quality thresholds for seedling irrigation (adapted for tropical and subtropical African conditions)
Parameter Ideal Acceptable Action required Typical African source at risk
EC (dS/m) < 0.5 0.5 â 0.75 > 0.75: blend or leach Boreholes in semi-arid zones
pH 6.0 â 7.0 5.5 â 7.5 Adjust with citric acid or lime Rift Valley alkaline boreholes
Sodium (SAR) < 3 3 â 6 > 6: avoid or blend Coastal and inland saline aquifers
Bicarbonate (meq/L) < 1.5 1.5 â 3.0 > 3.0: acidify Hard groundwater
Faecal coliforms (CFU/100 mL) 0 0 Treat before use Rivers, dams, open tanks

Source: FAO Irrigation and Drainage Paper 29 Rev. 1, Water Quality for Agriculture (Ayers & Westcot, 1985), thresholds adapted for seedling-stage sensitivity.

2. Manual Watering Techniques

For nurseries under 5,000 seedlings, manual watering with a rose-can or knapsack sprayer remains the most cost-effective method â provided the operator uses correct technique. The three failure modes are: (a) high-pressure pour that displaces seed and exposes roots, (b) watering at midday when evaporation losses reach 40â60%, and (c) uneven coverage where trays at the edge of the bench receive half the water of central trays.

Best practice: water before 09:00 or after 16:00; hold the rose 20â30 cm above the tray; pass twice in perpendicular directions; test moisture by inserting a finger 1 cm into the medium â it should feel like a wrung-out sponge, not dripping. For a knapsack sprayer, use a fine mist nozzle (0.8â1.2 mm orifice) and maintain 1â1.5 bar pressure.

3. Setting Up a Simple Drip Irrigation System

Drip irrigation is the business case for scaling. A gravity-fed system using a 200-litre raised drum (1.5 m head) can irrigate 2,000â4,000 seedlings through micro-tubing and spaghetti drippers at 1â2 L/hour per emitter. Capital cost in most African markets: USD 80â150 for a 100 mÂ² nursery. Payback is typically one to two seedling cycles because labour drops by 60â70% and water use by 30â50%.

Bill of materials (100 mÂ² nursery): 200 L drum (USD 25â40), 1.5 m stand (USD 15), 25 mm mainline PVC (USD 12), 16 mm drip lateral (USD 20), 40 micro-tubing drippers (USD 8), screen filter (USD 10), flush valve (USD 3). Total: USD 90â110.

4. Misting and Humidity Control

Germination and the first true-leaf stage require relative humidity above 80% at the medium surface. In hot, dry African conditions (e.g., Sudanian and Sahelian zones, or lowveld Zimbabwe), unprotected trays lose surface moisture within 30 minutes of watering. Solutions ranked by cost-effectiveness:

  • Low-cost: shade net (50â70%) plus morning misting with a hand sprayer â 2â3 passes at 07:00.
  • Mid-cost: low-tunnel polythene cover over germination trays, opened daily for 30 minutes to prevent fungal build-up.
  • Higher-cost: misting lines on a timer (2 minutes every 2 hours from 06:00 to 18:00) â justified only above 20,000 seedlings.

5. Avoiding Overwatering and Underwatering

Overwatering is the leading cause of seedling loss in African nurseries â not drought. Saturated media suffocate roots, promote Pythium and fungus gnats, and leach nutrients. Underwatering is easier to detect but causes irreversible cell damage within hours in high-VPD conditions.

Table 2: Diagnostic table for watering stress in seedlings
Symptom Likely cause Immediate action Preventive measure
Stem base pinched, dark, collapsed Damping-off (overwatering + pathogen) Remove affected trays; reduce watering; improve airflow Treat water; use sterile medium; water at 08:00
Leaves wilted at midday, recover by evening Mild water stress Increase morning irrigation volume Check emitter flow; adjust schedule
Leaves wilted permanently, crisp edges Severe underwatering Deep-water trays; shade for 24 h Install timer or increase frequency
Yellow lower leaves, stunted growth Nutrient leaching from overwatering Reduce volume; apply dilute foliar feed Water to container capacity, not runoff
Green algae on medium surface Persistent surface saturation Skip one cycle; increase airflow Water at root zone, not overhead

Source: Adapted from the University of Florida IFAS Extension, Seedling Production and Transplanting (HS 1200 series), and the African Orphan Crops Consortium nursery management guidelines (2019).

â  SAFETY WARNING â Water Treatment Chemicals

If you chlorinate irrigation water, never mix chlorine products with acids or ammonia-based fertilisers â toxic chlorine gas can be released. Store treatment chemicals away from seedlings, fertilisers, and fuel. Wear gloves and eye protection. In Kenya, Tanzania, Nigeria, and South Africa, chlorine for water treatment is regulated; use only food-grade calcium hypochlorite or sodium hypochlorite, and follow national pesticide/water-treatment registration rules. Never use agricultural pesticides in irrigation lines unless the label explicitly permits chemigation.

6. Watering Schedules by Growth Stage

Water demand scales with leaf area and root development. The table below gives baseline schedules for a tropical nursery (28â32Â°C daytime, 40â60% RH). Adjust upward by 20â30% in arid zones and downward in humid highlands.

Table 3: Stage-specific watering schedule for vegetable and tree seedlings (tropical conditions)
Stage Days after sowing Frequency Volume per tray (50 cells) Method
Germination 0 â 5 2Ã daily (07:00, 16:00) 0.5 â 0.8 L Fine mist
Cotyledon / emergence 6 â 12 1 â 2Ã daily 0.8 â 1.2 L Mist + light drip
True leaf 13 â 21 1Ã daily + check at noon 1.2 â 1.8 L Drip or rose-can
Hardening-off 22 â 30 1Ã daily, skip if rain 1.5 â 2.0 L Drip; reduce by 20%
Pre-transplant 2 days before Deep watering once 2.0 â 2.5 L Soak to container capacity

Source: Compiled from KALRO (Kenya) seedling production guidelines, IITA (Nigeria) horticulture training manuals, and the Horticultural Development Council of South Africa nursery best-practice notes.

Quick Reference Checklist

  1. Test your water source for EC, pH, and faecal coliforms at least once per season â before scaling production.
  2. Water before 09:00 and after 16:00 to cut evaporation losses by up to half.
  3. Use a fine rose or mist nozzle; never pour directly onto the medium surface.
  4. Insert a finger 1 cm into the medium â it should feel like a wrung-out sponge, never dripping wet.
  5. Flush drip lines weekly and clean the filter every 3 days to prevent emitter clogging.
  6. Maintain 80%+ surface humidity during germination using shade net or low tunnels.
  7. Remove and isolate any tray showing damping-off within 24 hours â do not compost it on-site.
  8. Log daily water volume and seedling mortality per tray; review weekly to catch drift early.

Further Reading (Free Official Resources)

  • FAO â Irrigation Water Management: Irrigation Water Needs (Training Manual No. 3)
  • FAO â Crop Evapotranspiration: Guidelines for Computing Crop Water Requirements (Paper 56)
  • University of Florida IFAS Extension â EDIS Seedling Production Publications
  • KALRO â Kenya Agricultural and Livestock Research Organization (nursery and horticulture technical briefs)
  • IITA â International Institute of Tropical Agriculture (seedling and horticulture training resources)

Business takeaway: A well-designed drip system plus a tested water source turns watering from a daily guess into a measurable input cost. Track litres per 1,000 seedlings and cost per litre; in most African markets, a nursery that reduces water and labour by 40% while lifting transplant survival from 70% to 90% adds 25â35% to gross margin per cycle â without adding a single square metre of production area.

quiz.q: What is the best water source for seedlings?
quiz.explanation: Rainwater is soft, free of chemicals, and ideal for seedlings.

quiz.q: How long should you let tap water sit to allow chlorine to evaporate?
quiz.explanation: Chlorine in tap water evaporates within 24 hours if left in an open container.

quiz.q: What does a TDS meter measure?
quiz.explanation: TDS stands for total dissolved solids, which indicates salt and mineral levels.

quiz.q: What is the recommended maximum TDS level for seedling water?
quiz.explanation: Aim for less than 500 ppm to avoid salt stress in seedlings.

quiz.q: Which tool is best for gentle watering of small seedlings?
options: B) Watering can with fine rose
quiz.explanation: A fine rose breaks the water flow and prevents disturbing seedlings.

quiz.q: When is the best time to water seedlings?
quiz.explanation: Morning watering allows leaves to dry before evening, reducing disease risk.

quiz.q: How can you check if a pot needs watering?
options: A) Lift the pot to feel weight
quiz.explanation: A light pot indicates dry soil, while a heavy pot indicates moisture.

quiz.q: What is a sign of overwatering?
options: C) Soil pulling away from pot
quiz.explanation: Overwatered seedlings often wilt because roots cannot breathe in soggy soil.

quiz.q: What is a sign of underwatering?
quiz.explanation: Underwatered seedlings have dry, crispy leaves and slow growth.

quiz.q: How deep should you check soil moisture with your finger?
quiz.explanation: Checking 2 cm deep gives a good indication of moisture around the root zone.

quiz.q: What is the benefit of drip irrigation?
quiz.explanation: Drip irrigation applies water directly to roots, reducing waste and labour.

quiz.q: What is needed to create pressure in a gravity-fed drip system?
quiz.explanation: Elevating the water tank at least 1 metre provides enough pressure for drip lines.

quiz.q: How often should you flush drip lines?
quiz.explanation: Weekly flushing prevents clogging from sediment and algae.

quiz.q: What is a simple DIY emitter material?
quiz.explanation: A plastic bottle with small holes can serve as a makeshift drip emitter.

quiz.q: What is the ideal relative humidity for most seedlings?
quiz.explanation: Most seedlings thrive at 60-80% relative humidity.

quiz.q: What is a sign of too much humidity?
quiz.explanation: Excessive humidity encourages fungal growth and mould on leaves and soil.

quiz.q: How can you increase humidity around seedlings?
quiz.explanation: Wet gravel or a humidome increases local humidity by evaporation.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of misting?
options: A) To water the soil deeply
quiz.explanation: Misting adds moisture to the air and leaf surface, raising humidity.

quiz.q: When should you avoid misting?
quiz.explanation: Misting in the evening can leave leaves wet overnight, promoting disease.

quiz.q: What is a simple tool to monitor humidity?
quiz.explanation: A hygrometer measures relative humidity.

quiz.q: What is the first step to avoid overwatering?
quiz.explanation: Checking soil moisture before watering prevents unnecessary watering.

quiz.q: What should you do if water pools on the soil surface?
options: B) Stop and let it soak
quiz.explanation: Pausing allows water to infiltrate and prevents runoff.

quiz.q: What is a good soil mix for drainage?
quiz.explanation: Adding sand or perlite improves drainage and prevents waterlogging.

quiz.q: How often should you water germinating seeds?
options: B) Twice a day with mist
quiz.explanation: Germinating seeds need constant moisture, so mist twice daily.

quiz.q: What is bottom watering?
quiz.explanation: Bottom watering involves soaking trays from below to encourage deep roots.

quiz.q: When should you reduce watering frequency?
quiz.explanation: Rainy season provides natural moisture, so reduce watering.

quiz.q: What is hardening off?
quiz.explanation: Hardening off involves gradually exposing seedlings to less water and outdoor conditions.

quiz.q: How long should you run a drip system for young seedlings?
quiz.explanation: 10-15 minutes is usually sufficient for young seedlings, but check soil moisture.

quiz.q: What is a sign of healthy seedlings?
options: B) Firm stems and green leaves
quiz.explanation: Firm stems and green leaves indicate proper watering and health.

quiz.q: What should you do if you see algae on soil?
quiz.explanation: Algae indicates excess moisture, so reduce watering frequency.
